category.label: Melatonin
category.comparisonNote: The 1 mg quantity is a cost comparison unit, not an intake recommendation. Check exact strength, release formulation and other ingredients. Higher strength or lower ingredient cost does not establish better sleep or suitability.

guide.title: Melatonin: body-clock timing before stronger sleep products
guide.summary: Melatonin is a hormone involved in the sleep-wake cycle. The reason, timing and release profile matter more than choosing the largest milligram number.
guide.evidence: Evidence is more relevant to circadian problems such as jet lag and some delayed sleep-wake phase cases than to all poor sleep. In a four-week trial, clinically assessed delayed-phase patients improved with melatonin plus behavioural scheduling. AASM suggests against using melatonin for chronic adult insomnia; CBT-I is an initial treatment to discuss.
guide.limitations: Short trials and specific sleep disorders do not establish benefit for every sleep complaint. Long-term safety remains uncertain. A gummy, strip, immediate-release tablet and prolonged-release product cannot be assumed to give the same exposure or outcome.
guide.catalogReading: Read melatonin milligrams per verified label serving, units per serving and release description. Keep other sedating ingredients separate. Cost per common milligram amount is a price calculation, not an intake recommendation, and more melatonin is not automatically better.
guide.safety: Possible effects include daytime drowsiness, headache and dizziness. Do not drive or use machinery when drowsy. Review medicines, especially blood thinners, and epilepsy with a clinician. Pregnancy and breastfeeding safety data are limited. Children need pediatric guidance; keep every form, including gummies, out of reach.
guide.author: Supplement Research editorial synthesis
bodySteps: Darkness normally promotes melatonin release from the brain's pineal gland, providing a biological night-time signal; evening light can suppress this signal.

Swallowed melatonin is absorbed and undergoes substantial first-pass processing in the liver. Different release systems can change its exposure pattern; milligram content alone does not describe that pattern.
Melatonin acts at receptors involved in sleep and circadian regulation. The effect depends on the sleep problem and timing; taking a product does not diagnose a low melatonin level.
guide.treatment: Melatonin can form part of professionally planned care for selected circadian disorders. It is not a cure for chronic insomnia, stress or sleep apnoea. Persistent poor sleep or excessive daytime sleepiness warrants assessment of its cause.
guide.whoMayBenefit: Some people with jet lag or a clinically assessed circadian delay may benefit from an appropriate plan. Children with sleep disorders require pediatric assessment, not selection from adult retail strengths. A short night of sleep alone does not establish a need.
guide.routineUse: No one should assume they need nightly melatonin indefinitely. Review the indication, sleep schedule and continuing benefit with a clinician. Behavioural treatment and light/sleep timing can be central, and melatonin is not an automatic addition to a sleep stack.

whoCanConsider: Adults managing travel across time zones who have checked whether a timed jet-lag plan fits their journey.
Adults with clinically assessed delayed sleep-wake phase who are following a sleep and light-timing plan.
whoShouldReview: People with epilepsy or blood-thinner treatment need medical supervision; review other medicines too.
Children, pregnant or breastfeeding people and older adults with dementia need appropriate professional review.
Persistent insomnia, daytime sleepiness or repeated need for sleep products warrants assessment of the cause.
buyingGuide.foodSummary: Tart cherries can contain trace melatonin, with amounts differing by cultivar. Ordinary food is not a predictable, clinically timed melatonin dose, and cherries are not an established cure for insomnia.

value.targetedUse: Adult jet lag or a professionally assessed delayed sleep-wake phase.
value.reason: A selected body-clock problem offers a clearer reason to consider melatonin than a general nightly sleep stack. Timing and the diagnosis matter; chronic insomnia has different treatment priorities.
worthWhen: There is a defined circadian goal and an appropriate timing plan.
Benefit and ongoing need will be reviewed rather than increasing strength automatically.
skipWhen: Sleep is already adequate or the aim is simply stronger sedation.
Persistent insomnia is being managed by indefinite self-escalation instead of assessment and behavioural treatment.
value.scope: Editorial priority for the stated adult circadian uses, not a validated efficacy score. It does not endorse a retail strength, pediatric use or routine long-term treatment.

dos.title: Start with a defined sleep question
dos.detail: A circadian goal and appropriate timing plan matter more than buying a stronger sleep product.

dos.title: Check the release and serving
dos.detail: Read melatonin per label serving, units per serving and other sedating ingredients; reassess benefit and ongoing need.

donts.title: Don't equate strength with better sleep
donts.detail: A lower cost per milligram is arithmetic, not evidence that a higher amount suits your situation.

donts.title: Don't ignore drowsiness or persistent symptoms
donts.detail: Avoid driving when drowsy; persistent insomnia needs assessment rather than indefinite self-escalation.

intakeGuide.summary: No nutritional requirement. Indication, timing and formulation matter; a sleep problem needs assessment before a personal regimen.
notes: No automatic dose increase is assigned for training frequency or experience.

medicalGuide.summary: Condition-specific evidence, separate from sports benefits and purchase priority.

conditions.findings: Timed use may be part of professionally planned care; diagnosis, timing and formulation are central.
conditions.limits: Melatonin can form part of professionally planned care for selected circadian disorders. It is not a cure for chronic insomnia, stress or sleep apnoea. Persistent poor sleep or excessive daytime sleepiness warrants assessment of its cause.

conditions.findings: Melatonin is not an established remedy for sleep apnoea; chronic insomnia requires assessment and evidence-based care.

pathway.title: Oral melatonin adds to a timing signal
pathway.summary: Natural melatonin signals biological night. An oral product must first be absorbed and pass through the liver before the remaining hormone reaches receptors.

tracks.label: Oral absorption, clearance and receptor signalling

steps.label: The oral formulation releases melatonin
steps.detail: Melatonin is absorbed after administration; release formulation affects the timing of exposure.

steps.label: Liver processing reduces oral availability
steps.detail: Substantial first-pass hepatic metabolism means only part of an oral dose reaches systemic circulation unchanged.

steps.label: Remaining melatonin reaches the circulation
steps.detail: Circulating exposure depends on absorption, metabolism and the product's release characteristics.

steps.label: Melatonin receptors receive the timing signal
steps.detail: Melatonin acts at MT1 and MT2 receptors involved in biological timing and sleep-related responses.

pathway.caveat: Receptor activity does not mean a higher dose gives better sleep. Timing, the sleep problem and other medicines change how the product should be assessed.
